threads.thread_goal: Align on current guest journey and agree on main pain points to fix first.

messages.text: Morning all. I have posted a first draft of the current guest journey in A1 based on T1, from when guests arrive at the door through to departure. It includes what we do at the door, luggage handling, when the contact centre gets involved, and where we see delays or complaints today. Can the porters take a look and call out any missing steps or things that do not match what really happens on shift, especially at busy check-in and late-night arrivals

Thanks for sharing. First read of A1 looks close to what I see on day shifts. One gap: for coach arrivals we often have a quick pre-arrival call from the organiser to the contact centre, and we pre-tag luggage in the lobby before guests go to reception. That step is not in the flow yet. Also, for late check-ins after 23:00, we sometimes hold luggage in the side room while we wait for security to clear the guest if there is any concern. That handoff is also missing.

I went through A1 as well. On busy Friday evenings, after greeting, we often park cars first before tagging luggage, just to clear the driveway. The draft shows tagging before parking. In practice we sometimes skip writing the room number on the tag until later, once the guest has checked in. That is a point where bags can get mixed up. Might be worth calling that out as a pain point.

From my side, the departure part in A1 is a bit short. Often guests call down from the room to request help with luggage, and the call goes to the contact centre first, not reception. We then radio the porter station. That extra hop is not shown. Also, for early airport runs, we sometimes store luggage overnight near the door for quick loading. That storage step is not in the map.

I noticed in A1 that after a complaint at the door, it jumps straight to contact centre escalation. In reality, we usually try a quick fix first, like offering to carry bags up immediately or calling reception to speed up check-in. Only if the guest is still upset do we call the contact centre supervisor. Maybe we should show that quick fix step so it is clear what is expected.

One more thing on arrivals: for guests with visible mobility issues, we often bring a chair to the lobby and let them sit while we handle check-in with reception over the phone. That is not in A1. Not sure if it belongs in this general flow or later in the special needs guide, but it is a real step we take today.

This is helpful. I will update A1 to add: pre-arrival organiser call and lobby pre-tagging for coach groups, the late-night luggage hold with security check, the quick fix step before escalation, and the early departure call flow via the contact centre. For the mobility support, I suggest we keep a simple note in A1 and then go deeper in the special needs work under T5. Any other pain points we should highlight while we are editing

On pain points, the three that stand out for me from A1 and recent shifts are: 1) Luggage mix-ups when tags are filled in late or not at all during busy arrivals. 2) Guests waiting at the door while we try to find someone on the radio to confirm room readiness. 3) Complaints that get bounced between porter, reception, and contact centre because it is not clear who owns the follow-up. If we focus the first rollout on those, I think we will see fewer complaints quickly.

I agree with those three. I would maybe add long waits for cars from valet at checkout, but that might be harder to fix quickly. The luggage tags and unclear ownership are the ones guests complain about the most at the door.

From my side, the radio wait is the most painful. Sometimes we stand with the guest for several minutes trying to get an answer on room readiness. If the new checklist and escalation matrix can give us a faster path, that would help a lot.

Just to confirm, in A1 for departures, do we want to show when we proactively ask guests about transport while they are checking out, or is that considered optional service I am asking because sometimes we skip it when the line is long, and that can lead to last-minute rush requests at the door.

Good question. For A1, I suggest we show the typical path, including the proactive transport question at checkout, and we can later decide in the checklist how strongly we want to push that step during peak times. That way the map reflects what we aim for, not just what happens on the toughest days.

One last detail: when guests arrive with food deliveries at the same time as check-in, we often pause the luggage process to check hygiene and security rules at the door. That is a small step but it can delay the flow. Might be worth a note in A1 under arrival exceptions.

Noted, I will add a short branch in A1 for arrivals with external food or packages, with a reminder that we follow existing hygiene and security checks before moving luggage. I will also highlight the three priority pain points called out above so they are clear for the next tasks under T2 and T3.

Once you have updated A1, can you confirm that we will treat it as the baseline for the checklist and script work I want to make sure we do not keep changing the map while we are already drafting A2 and A3.

Yes, that makes sense. I will incorporate all comments into A1 today and then freeze it as our current-state view for this project. Any future tweaks can go into a later version, but for T2, T3, and T6 we will use this updated A1 as the reference.
Works for me. Once A1 is updated, I will use it to check that the arrival part of the porter checklist covers the real steps we take at the door.
Same here. Having a fixed map will help when we look at how complaints move between us and the contact centre later.

threads.thread_goal: Co-create and finalise the porter arrival and luggage handling checklist.

messages.text: I have put together a first draft of the porter arrival and luggage handling checklist in A2, based on what we mapped in A1 and the expectations in T2. It covers greeting, quick scan for special needs, luggage tagging, parking, room delivery, and a short departure section. I am less sure about where to place the door security checks so they do not slow us down. Can you all review and suggest changes, especially around the order of steps and any missing checks

Thanks for drafting A2. Overall structure looks good. I would suggest we lock in this order for arrivals: 1) Greet and confirm booking name. 2) Quick visual check for special needs or security concerns. 3) Tag luggage fully before moving it, even if the room is not ready yet. 4) Confirm room readiness via radio or system. 5) Either escort guest and luggage to room or store luggage with clear location noted. For door security, I would place the main check right after greeting, before we handle luggage, so we do not have to backtrack.

From the contact centre side, A2 aligns with what we want to see when we get calls about missing luggage. The key for us is that the tag is complete and the storage location is written down. Could we make those fields mandatory in the checklist, maybe with a small reminder that incomplete tags are one of the top pain points we picked in TH1

Looking at A2, I am wondering where we note if security has been called for a guest we are unsure about. Right now it just says 'contact security if needed'. Should we add a tick box to confirm that we informed them and maybe a space to write the time This might help later if there is an incident.

On the departure part of A2, we currently have 'ask about transport' as the last step. In practice, I think we should move that earlier, right after greeting the guest at the door, so we can call a taxi or bring the car around while we handle luggage. That might reduce the rush at the end.

I like the idea of a clear door security step, but I am a bit worried about slowing down coach arrivals. Maybe we can have a short version for groups, where we do a quick scan and rely more on the organiser, and a fuller check for individual guests. Could A2 show that difference without becoming too long

Maybe we can solve that by keeping one main checklist in A2, but adding a small note under the door security step: for groups, do a quick scan and rely on organiser list, for individuals, follow the full check. That way we do not create two separate flows, but we still recognise the difference.

Thanks all, this helps. I will rework A2 so that: door security check comes right after greeting, with a short note for groups; luggage tagging is always completed before moving bags; there is a tick box for when we call security, with time; and the departure section asks about transport earlier. I will keep the wording simple so it still fits on one page.

Once you have that version, I can do a quick pass to check that the steps line up with the escalation matrix in A6 and that we are not asking porters to call the contact centre for things that should go straight to security or reception. Then we can confirm the final order of steps.

When you update A2, can you also add a small reminder under the storage step to log the luggage in the issue log A4 during the pilot That will help us track if the new process is reducing lost bag complaints.
Good point, I had not linked A2 to A4 yet. I will add a short note to log stored luggage in the issue log during the pilot, at least for the first weeks, so we can see patterns.

On the door security part, can we be explicit that we do not block the entrance while we check IDs For example, we can step slightly aside with the guest while keeping the door clear for others. Maybe a short reminder in A2 would avoid queues building up.

I also wonder if we should include a quick line about hygiene when handling wet or dirty luggage, like after rain. Maybe just a reminder to use gloves or wipes if needed, so we stay aligned with hygiene rules without adding a full new section.
I can add a short hygiene reminder under the luggage handling step, yes. I will keep it brief so the checklist stays readable.

Once these edits are in, I am comfortable saying the sequence in A2 is final: greet, door security scan, special needs check, full luggage tagging, confirm room readiness, then either escort or store with log entry. If no one objects, we can treat that as the agreed order for the pilot.
Agreed from my side. The placement of the door security check right after greeting, with the group note, feels like the right balance between safety and speed.
No objections here. Happy to test this version of A2 during the weekend pilot.

threads.thread_goal: Agree on complaint handling script and escalation matrix across teams.

messages.text: I have uploaded draft versions of the complaint handling script in A3 and the escalation matrix in A6, based on T3, T4, and T6. The script follows a simple structure: opening, listening, probing, proposing a solution, and closing. The matrix shows who to contact first and second for typical issues, with day, evening, and night variations. Can porters review and tell me if the wording feels natural at the door and if the escalation paths match what is realistic on shift

I went through A3 and A6. The structure of the script works well. I like that it starts with a clear apology and then a short summary of what the guest is upset about. One suggestion: for luggage issues, can we add a line that we will check the issue log A4 before calling the contact centre That might avoid bouncing the guest around if the problem is already recorded.

In A3, some of the phrases feel a bit formal for the door, like 'I will now take ownership of your concern'. I usually say something simpler, like 'Let me sort this out for you'. Could we include a few more everyday options so it does not sound scripted

On the escalation matrix A6, for noise complaints at night it currently says to call the contact centre first. In practice, we usually call security directly if it is after 23:00 and the guest seems very upset. Maybe the night column should reflect that, with security as first contact and contact centre second.

For complaints about long waits for cars at checkout, A6 points to the contact centre. I think it should go to valet or front office first, since they control the keys. The contact centre can help if we need to log a formal complaint, but they cannot speed up the car directly.

In A3, the closing step suggests we always offer something extra, like a drink voucher. That is not always possible at the door without approval. Could we adjust the wording so that we first try to fix the issue, and only offer extras if a supervisor or front office manager agrees

These are good points. I will update A3 to include simpler phrase options, like the one you suggested, and make the closing step clear that any extras need approval. For A6, I will switch night-time noise complaints to security first, and change car wait complaints to front office or valet first. I will also add a reminder in the luggage section to check A4 before escalating.

One more suggestion for A3: in the probing step, can we add a short question about whether this has happened to the guest before during their stay That helps us spot repeated issues and bring them to the weekly review under T11.

For the opening line in A3, I like 'I am sorry this has happened, let me see what we can do right now'. It feels natural and still shows we are taking it seriously. Maybe we can list that as the main option.

On A6, for complaints about special needs not being met, like missing wheelchair support, who should be first contact The matrix shows contact centre, but often we need housekeeping or security involved too.

Good catch. For special needs complaints, I suggest we set front office as first contact, with contact centre second, and note in A6 that they may involve housekeeping or security depending on the case. The detailed steps will sit in A5, but the matrix should still show who we call first.

For evening shifts, A6 currently has the same path as daytime for most issues. In reality, we have fewer managers around. Maybe we should show the contact centre supervisor as first escalation for general complaints after 20:00, except for safety or security issues.
I agree with that. On late shifts we often rely on the contact centre supervisor to decide if we log a formal complaint or just fix it on the spot.

Understood. I will adjust the evening column in A6 so that for general service complaints the contact centre supervisor is first escalation, with front office manager second if available. Safety and security issues will still go to security first at all times.

Once these edits are in, I think A3 will be ready to use. The structure is clear, and the language feels more natural. I suggest we confirm this version as our standard script for both porters and contact centre, and then test it in a few role-plays before the pilot.
I am comfortable with that. The updated A3 feels like something I can actually say at the door without sounding stiff.

For A6, with the changes you described, the day, evening, and night paths now match what we actually do: front office or valet for cars, security first for safety, contact centre supervisor for general complaints in the evening, and security first for noise at night. I think we can treat this as the agreed matrix.
Great, I will lock in the current versions of A3 and A6 as final for this rollout and use them to update the quick reference guide and the training huddles plan.

threads.thread_goal: Define approach for special needs guests and shift handovers before pilot.

messages.text: I have drafted two documents for review: A5, which lists common special needs scenarios and steps for porters and contact centre under T5, and A8, a shift handover template for porters under T12. A5 covers mobility support, visual or hearing impairments, vulnerable guests, and guests showing signs of substance misuse. A8 focuses on open guest requests, luggage in storage, and any incidents to flag. Can you check if these cover what you see on shift and if there are any gaps before we finalise them for the pilot

Looking at A5, the mobility and visual impairment sections look good. For guests who seem under the influence, it currently says to call security and the contact centre. In practice, we usually call security first and keep the guest near the lobby, not at the door. Maybe we should be clearer about not letting them wander near the entrance for safety.

On A5, for guests with hearing impairments, could we add a note to use written notes or show the complaint script visually if needed Right now it just says 'speak clearly and slowly'. Some guests prefer to read.

For vulnerable guests travelling alone, like young people arriving late at night, A5 suggests we inform the contact centre. Should we also note that we log this in the issue log A4 so that the night team is aware during handover

On A8, I like the sections for open requests and luggage in storage. Could we add a small field for 'special needs guests to watch' so that the next shift knows who might need extra attention For example, guests with mobility issues on high floors or guests who had a serious complaint.

From the contact centre side, A5 looks aligned with our current practice, but I agree we should be explicit that security is first contact for substance misuse or safety concerns. For A8, I would also suggest a small tick box to confirm that any open complaints from A4 have been mentioned in the handover.

Thanks all, this is useful. I will update A5 so that: security is clearly first contact for substance misuse, with a note to keep the guest away from the entrance; the hearing impairment section mentions written notes and showing key parts of the script; and vulnerable guests are logged in A4 and flagged in A8. For A8, I will add a 'special needs or vulnerable guests' field and a tick box for open complaints.

For mobility support in A5, can we also mention that we should offer to bring check-in closer to the guest, for example by calling reception instead of asking them to queue That is something we already do but it would be good to make it standard.
On the vulnerable guests part, should we specify any age range or just say 'guests who appear at risk' I do not want us to make assumptions, but some guidance would help.

I would keep it as 'guests who appear at risk' and give a few examples in A5, like very young guests travelling alone late at night, guests who seem disoriented, or guests who report feeling unsafe. That keeps it practical without turning it into a strict rule.
On A8, when do we expect porters to fill it in Exactly at every shift change, or only when there are open items I want to be sure we all use it the same way.
I would suggest we use A8 at every shift handover, even if it is mostly empty, so that it becomes a habit. It should not take long if there are no open requests.

I agree. Let us make it standard that A8 is used at every porter shift handover, with a quick run-through of open requests, stored luggage, incidents, and any special needs or vulnerable guests. That way we do not miss anything, even on quieter days.

From my side, the updated A5 covers the key scenarios we see in the contact centre as well. I suggest we treat the steps in A5 as mandatory for mobility, visual or hearing impairments, and guests who appear at risk, with room for judgement on how we phrase things to guests.
I am fine with that. The steps in A5 match what we try to do already, just more clearly written down.
Using A8 at every handover works for me. It should help avoid surprises with stored luggage and special cases.

threads.thread_goal: Plan and review the weekend pilot and training huddles outcomes.

messages.text: Sharing the plan for the weekend pilot and training huddles, based on T7 and T8. The huddles will be 10 minutes at the start of each shift from Friday evening to Sunday night, using the quick reference guide A7 and walking through A2, A3, and the key parts of A5 and A6. The pilot focus is on the three pain points we agreed in TH1: complete luggage tagging, faster confirmation of room readiness, and clear ownership of complaints. During the pilot, we will log issues in A4 and do a short review under T11 on Monday. Please confirm this focus still makes sense before we lock the schedule.

The focus still matches what we see on shift. I would just add that during the huddles we briefly remind everyone how to use A8 for handovers, since that will be important over the weekend when shifts turn over quickly.

I am ok with the focus. For the huddles, could we have a simple example for each pain point, like a short role-play for a luggage mix-up and a complaint at the door That would help people remember the script in A3.
On the pilot logging in A4, do we want every small delay recorded, or only when a guest complains I am asking because on busy Saturdays we might not have time to log every minor delay.
For the weekend pilot, should we also track how often we actually use the new script in A3 Maybe a small tick box in A4 when we handle a complaint using the script.

On the huddle schedule, can we confirm times for the night shifts I want to make sure the 23:00 and 07:00 teams also get a quick run-through of A2 and A3, since they see a lot of late arrivals and early departures.

For A4 during the pilot, let us focus on logging cases where the guest complains or where the delay is more than five minutes. That should keep it manageable while still giving us useful data for the review under T11.

For night shifts, I propose we run the huddles at 23:00 and 07:00, right after shift start, using the same A7 guide. We will keep them to 10 minutes and focus on arrivals, departures, and the escalation paths in A6 that are specific to night.

I can help prepare two short role-play scenarios for the huddles: one for a luggage mix-up and one for a long wait at the door. We can base them directly on A3 and the flows in A1 so they feel realistic.

Good idea on tracking script usage. I will add a simple tick box in A4 for 'script used' whenever we log a complaint. That will help us see if using A3 correlates with faster resolution or fewer repeat complaints.
The five-minute rule for logging in A4 sounds reasonable. During the pilot, I will keep a small notepad at the door to jot down times and then transfer them into the log when things are quieter.
Works for me too. I will remind the team on the evening shift to use A4 for any complaint or delay over five minutes.
Thanks for confirming the night huddle times. I will make sure the night team has printed copies of A7 and A2 at the porter station before Friday.

To summarise, the weekend pilot will focus on the three agreed pain points from TH1, use the approved checklist A2 and complaint script A3, follow the escalation matrix A6, and log relevant issues in A4. Huddles will run at the start of each shift using A7, and we will review results on Monday under T11. Unless there are objections, we will go ahead with this plan.
No objections from me. I will coordinate with the porter teams to make sure everyone knows the focus and where to find A2, A3, A5, A6, A7, and A8 at the station.
All clear. I will share feedback from the door after the weekend so we can capture it in the Monday review.
